Kernel Order Tuning

Source: vignettes/kernel-order-tuning.Rmd
kernel-order-tuning.Rmd

The order s controls localization: larger values concentrate weight closer to the reporting profile. A grid compares estimates across orders and retains its specified default; it does not select an optimal order. The paper gives the statistical motivation and inference conditions.

Fit and compare a grid 

demo <- np_demo_data(n = 200, p = 2, seed = 1)
fit <- np_dnn(
  data = demo$data, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y",
  x0 = demo$x0, tuning_mode = "grid"
)
fit$tuning_grid$candidates
#>   candidate_id computed_key is_default feasible reason status lambda  s
#> 1   lambda_0p3         s_15      FALSE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.30 15
#> 2   lambda_0p4         s_21       TRUE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.40 21
#> 3   lambda_0p5         s_26      FALSE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.50 26
#> 4  lambda_0p75         s_39      FALSE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.75 39
fit$tuning_grid$estimates
#>   candidate_id computed_key lambda  s target_id component  estimate         se
#> 1   lambda_0p3         s_15   0.30 15         1      <NA> 0.1311178 0.08214191
#> 2   lambda_0p4         s_21   0.40 21         1      <NA> 0.1650251 0.08880114
#> 3   lambda_0p5         s_26   0.50 26         1      <NA> 0.1835091 0.09559482
#> 4  lambda_0p75         s_39   0.75 39         1      <NA> 0.2118122 0.11896597
#>   status reason
#> 1     ok     ok
#> 2     ok     ok
#> 3     ok     ok
#> 4     ok     ok

The main estimate remains the default candidate. Use a candidate view to inspect another order without fitting the nuisance functions again:

view <- candidate_fit(fit, 1L)
coef(view)
#>  target_1 
#> 0.1311178

Candidate identifiers refer to rows of the tuning grid, not just the resolved order. If two tuning settings resolve to the same s, they remain distinct candidates even when their computation is shared. Plot labels include their identifiers when needed to distinguish them. Candidate reconstruction validates the retained controls, target identities and cached ranks; refit an incomplete or inconsistent saved object.

CATE and CLATE use the same tuning_mode convention. See Getting started and Conditional LATE for their signal inputs. plot_tuning(fit) draws the sensitivity comparison when ggplot2 is installed.

Inspect the default rule

The built-in rule is floor(lambda * n^((kx + 1)/(kx + 2))), with lambda = 0.4 and sensitivity multipliers c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.75). Here kx is the number of reporting covariates. lambda = 1 remains an available, more concentrated localization setting. Delete-one uncertainty requires s < n.

tun <- tuning_dnn_paper()
tuning_eval(tun, n = 1000, kx = 2, k = 1)$s
#> [1] 71
tuning_eval(tun, n = 1000, kx = 2, k = 1, mode = "grid")$candidates
#>   lambda   s feasible reason
#> 1   0.30  53     TRUE     ok
#> 2   0.40  71     TRUE     ok
#> 3   0.50  88     TRUE     ok
#> 4   0.75 133     TRUE     ok

Explicit s and a tuning specification are alternative inputs; grid mode cannot be combined with explicit s. Diagnostics record the resolved order and its provenance:

as.data.frame(diagnostics(fit))[, c("target_id", "tuning_name", "tuning_default_s")]
#>          target_id       tuning_name tuning_default_s
#> target_1  target_1 paper_undersmooth               21

Define and register a custom rule

For a fixed order, a small function is enough:

fixed12 <- as_tuning(function(...) 12L, name = "fixed_12")
tuning_eval(fixed12, n = 300, kx = 2, k = 1)$s
#> [1] 12
register_tuning("fixed_12", fixed12)
get_tuning("fixed_12")$name
#> [1] "fixed_12"

new_tuning() also accepts explicit candidate generation and metadata; see its help for the full interface. A custom rule must respect the estimator’s order constraints. DNN weights explains the resulting rank weights, and Notation and conventions lists the argument and result shapes.
